name: Pennsylvania Dutch (Lancaster County)
family: Indo-European, Germanic, West Germanic, High German, Rhine Franconian (Palatine base)
variety: Pennsylvania Dutch (Pennsylvania German) as spoken by the Old Order Amish and Old Order Mennonites of Lancaster County, Pennsylvania; text in the Buffington-Barba spelling
sources: Buffington, Albert F. and Barba, Preston A. (1954). A Pennsylvania German Grammar. Allentown: Schlechter's.
Frey, J. William (1942). A Simple Grammar of Pennsylvania Dutch. Clinton, South Carolina: Jacobs Press.
Reed, Carroll E. and Seifert, Lester W. (1954). A Linguistic Atlas of Pennsylvania German. Marburg.
Van Ness, Silke (1994). Pennsylvania German. In König and van der Auwera (eds.), The Germanic Languages. London: Routledge.
Louden, Mark L. (2016). Pennsylvania Dutch: The Story of an American Language. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.
Keiser, Steven Hartman (2012). Pennsylvania German in the American Midwest. Publication of the American Dialect Society 96. Durham: Duke University Press.
Kopp, Achim (1999). The Phonology of Pennsylvania German English as Evidence of Language Maintenance and Shift. Selinsgrove: Susquehanna University Press.
Fasold, Ralph W. (1980). The conversational function of Pennsylvania Dutch intonation. Paper presented at NWAVE IX, Ann Arbor.

Huffines, Marion Lois (1986). Intonation in language contact: Pennsylvania German English. In Enninger (ed.), Studies on the Languages and the Verbal Behavior of the Pennsylvania Germans I. Stuttgart: Steiner.
eSpeak NG voice and phoneme files for pdc (espeak-ng-data/lang/gmw/pdc, phsource/ph_pennsylvania_german, dictsource/pdc_rules), whose comments state the dialect features the voices assume.
contrasts: short versus long vowels, with a difference of quality: /ɪ/ versus /iː/, /ɛ/ versus /eː/, /ʊ/ versus /uː/, /ʌ/ versus /oː/, /ɑ/ versus /ɔː/
no front rounded vowels: the vowels of German schön, Tür, böse, Feuer are unrounded (schee, Dier, bees, Feier)
long /æː/ (written ae: Kaes, Baer) versus /eː/ (written ee: schee)
back rounded long /ɔː/ (written aa: Baam, Fraa, Daag) versus /oː/ (written oo: Schprooch)
palatal and velar fricatives [ç x] and the weak voiced fricative [ɣ] between back vowels (saage, Waage)
lexical stress in prefixed words and loans
allophony: the lenis stops /b d ɡ/ are voiceless unaspirated lenes in the older descriptions; the historical fortis /p t/ fell together with them in native words (Disch 'table', Dochder 'daughter', Babbier 'paper'), while /k/ stays aspirated before a vowel (Kuh, Katz) and is lenis before a consonant (glee 'small', Gnoche 'bone')

between vowels, historical /b/ is [v] (hawwe, gewwe, Lewe) and historical /ɡ/ is [j] after front vowels, /r/ and /l/ (Reege [ˈreːjə]; the word for German morgen has [j]) and [ɣ] after back vowels (saage [ˈsɔːɣə])
onset /r/ is the American English approximant [ɹ] for most present-day Lancaster speakers; older and eastern speech has a tongue-tip tap or trill
/r/ after a vowel is vocalised to [ɐ] or lost, giving centring diphthongs (Bier [biːɐ], Ohr [oːɐ]) and a final [ɐ] for -er (Wasser [ˈvɑsɐ])
/l/ is velarised [ɫ] after a vowel, as in American English
au is a long monophthong [aː] in present-day sectarian speech according to the voice files (Haus [haːs], Maul [maːl]); older descriptions give a diphthong [aʊ]
ei is a diphthong [aɪ], but Keiser (2012) reports that Pennsylvania speakers monophthongise it before /r/ and /l/ (the 'Lancaster rule')
front vowels before a vocalised /r/ are lowered to [æː] according to the voice files (Baer, Kaer)
ch is palatal [ç] after front vowels and consonants and velar [x] after back vowels (ich, Millich, Buch)
s is voiceless in all positions, also word-initially (sehne), and is [ʃ] before p and t (Schprooch, bischt)
obstruents are voiceless at the end of a word (Daag [dɔːk])
a vowel is inserted between /r/ or /l/ and a following velar or palatal consonant, and the spelling shows it (darich, Barig, Millich, schtarick)
unstressed e is schwa; unstressed -er is [ɐ]
English loans are frequent and are said with English sounds, among them [ɹ], [w], [dʒ], [z] and [θ], to a degree that depends on the speaker
phonotactics: onset clusters with /ʃ/ before p, t, m, n, l, r, w and with /ɡ/ or /k/ before n and l (Gnoche, glee); prefix vowel loss gives clusters such as gsch- and gf- (Gschwischder, gfalle)
final unstressed -n of German is lost (wasche, schee, Schtee)
short stressed vowels are followed by a consonant, which the spelling doubles; open stressed syllables have long vowels

stress.rule: Stress falls on the first syllable of the stem; the prefixes ge-, be-, ver- (fer-), er-, zer- are unstressed, separable particles and the first member of a compound are stressed, the suffix -erei is stressed, and loans keep the stress of the source word (Babbier on the second syllable).
stress.cues: pitch movement, duration and intensity; unstressed syllables have schwa or [ɐ]

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong: unstressed syllables mostly have [ə] or [ɐ], and unstressed prefix vowels are often lost (gsund, gfalle)
rhythm.notes: No instrumental rhythm measurements are known to me.

length.notes: Vowel length is contrastive and tied to quality. Double consonant letters mark a short vowel; consonants are not long.

intonation.declarative: peaks on accented syllables, final fall to low
intonation.yes_no_question: rise to the last accented syllable followed by a fall on the syllables after it (a final rise-fall), the pattern that Pennsylvania Dutch has passed on to the English of the region
intonation.wh_question: accent on the question word, final fall
intonation.continuation: rise or high level at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: peak on the accented syllable followed by a fall
intonation.notes: The yes-no question pattern is from Fasold (1980) and Huffines (1986). The rest is low confidence: I know of no instrumental study of statement intonation in Pennsylvania Dutch.

problems: the stops b, d, g are inherited from the German table and are fully voiced; the descriptions have voiceless lenis stops
yes-no questions use tune q4, which ends in a rise; the documented pattern is a rise to the accented syllable followed by a final fall
ei stays [aɪ] before /r/ and /l/ (Eil, Meil, Scheier), where Keiser reports monophthongs for Pennsylvania speakers
stress is put on the first syllable of words that carry it later (Babbier is [ˈbɑbiːɐ])

English loans that keep their English spelling are read by the German-type letter rules (computer is [ˈkʌmpuːtɐ]); the pronunciation list has about 260 entries, mostly letters, symbols, numbers and function words
postvocalic /l/ uses the dark l of the English table and onset /l/ the clear one, which fits the voice notes, but there is no way to choose the older clear l and tapped r within this voice
the pronunciations have not been checked by native speakers (the voice is marked 'testing')
good: the unrounded vowel system, [ɔː] for aa, [æː] for ae and [ʌ] for short o follow the descriptions
vocalised r with centring diphthongs and [ɐ] for -er
intervocalic g is [j] or [ɣ] by the preceding vowel, ww is [v], final obstruents are devoiced
unstressed prefixes ge-, be-, ver-, er-, zer- and stressed particles are handled by rules
the three regional voices share one rule file with conditional rules, so dialect differences stay explicit

notes: Statements about au, about /r/ and /l/ and about the lowering before r follow the eSpeak NG voice files together with Keiser (2012), who treats /aɪ/, /r/ and /l/ as the variables that separate Lancaster County from the Midwest, and Louden (2016). [aː] in the vowel list is the monophthong written au. Buffington and Barba describe the eastern nonsectarian speech of their time, which is closer to the Lehigh voice (pdc-x-lehigh). No formant, duration or voice onset time values have been published that I can quote.
